name: Juan Licerio
title: Juan Licerio
bio: I work across 3D, motion, projection mapping, and XR.
bioDetails: My passion lies in Emerging Media and Digital Art, where I continually develop and experiment with new technologies. My approach to art is informed by my studies in Architectural Design Technology and Software Engineering, which provide a structural and problem-solving framework.

My self-taught expertise includes a wide range of media: 3D art and animation such as detailed 3D artworks, logo renderings, and dynamic motion design, and immersive media, developing experiential works through projection mapping and actively exploring extended reality, including augmented reality and virtual reality. I focus on technically integrating these mediums to create high-quality, compelling visual experiences.

projects.title: Warp and Weft
projects.summary: A real-time WebGPU meadow cut into a checker, with one white chair as the only object.
projects.description: A field of grass blades is mown into a checker and one plastic chair stands on a dark square. 265,744 blades bend in the wind in real time, and the pointer parts them. Built in WebGPU with a film pass for halation, grain, and vignette.

caseStudy.brief: A WebGPU field of grass had to read as cloth. The scene needed one object, one checker cut, and no visible blade cards. The page had to run in a browser tab at full desktop width, hold a steady frame, and keep the chair readable at phone width. The field is the subject, and the chair is the scale reference.
process: A clump table and blade generators build the meadow. Each clump shares a colour field, so the checker reads at distance without a texture.
A vertex shader bends the blades in the wind. The wind runs on a slow noise field, and a pointer ray parts the grass around the cursor.
A mask cuts the field into a checker. The dark squares use a shorter blade and a cooler colour, so the pattern survives the camera move.
One GLB chair sits on a dark square. The chair is the only hard edge in the frame, and it gives the field a human scale.
A film pass adds halation, grain, and vignette. The grade stays low-contrast so the white chair holds against the grass.
The camera keeps a low eye height. The horizon stays out of frame, so the field reads as cloth rather than a landscape.
The drawing buffer caps at the viewport size, and the blade count stays fixed for each run. The phone layout keeps the chair readable without changing the scene geometry.
A small status line reports frame rate and blade count. The test run read 265,744 blades at 60 fps.
The GLB chair loads once and is drawn once. The meadow uses no textures; colour comes from the clump fields.
result: Runs at 60.2 fps at 1440 x 900 in headless Chrome 156, on the live canvas.
The phone run draws the same scene on a 359 x 478 canvas with no console error.
265,744 blades in the live scene.

projects.title: Viscous Orb
projects.summary: A fluid orb with a living dye trail, spectral rim, and a moving dither veil.
projects.description: A single glowing sphere holds a real-time fluid surface. Pointer motion and an invisible mover push velocity and dye through the field, and the surface settles after each pass. The veil turns the moving liquid into coarse Bayer pixels. The rim stays analytic, and no tiled texture is sampled in the reflection.

caseStudy.brief: A single sphere had to hold a real-time fluid interior and keep a clean silhouette. The earlier build used a tiled caustic texture, and the grid repeated in the reflection. The target was a liquid surface that reacts to a pointer, settles on its own, and holds 60 fps at portrait size. The page also had to run inside a portfolio iframe with a capped drawing buffer.
process: The study renders one sphere and one full-screen fluid pass. A pointer ray hits the sphere, and the hit point writes velocity and dye into a 256 x 256 field. An invisible mover crosses the orb on a loop, so the surface moves without input.
A pressure solve and a vorticity pass move the dye through the field. The velocity decays after each pass. The dye carries the colour, and the field returns to rest in about one second.
The first build sampled a tiled caustic texture. The tiles showed as a grid in the reflection. I removed the texture and drove the reflection from the fluid field. The grid artifact disappeared.
A Bayer veil reads the dye and turns the moving liquid into coarse pixels. The veil clears as the field settles. A toggle keeps the veil off for clean stills.
Bloom runs at quarter resolution with two blur passes. Soft focus mixes the blurred frame at 0.42. An analytic rim keeps the silhouette sharp while the interior stays soft.
The portfolio embed sets a 1728 px drawing buffer cap. The study scales the fluid field and the bloom pass to that cap, so the frame rate holds at desktop and phone width.
result: Runs at 59.5 fps at 1440 x 900 and 59.9 fps at 390 x 844 in headless Chrome 156.
The portfolio embed caps the drawing buffer at 1728 px.
The still shows the dither veil and the spectral rim. The touch frame shows the dye trail.

projects.title: Forget-me-not
projects.summary: Projection mapping and technical setup for the McAllen staging of Victoria Cantu's first solo exhibition at Ponte Creative Studio & Gallery.
projects.description: Provided technical setup and specialized support for this immersive light and video installation by Victoria. My role was projection mapping and technical integration. I was responsible for fitting the artist's video content onto the complex surfaces of the exhibition space, including the bed, walls, and sink.
projects.tools: Resolume and MadMapper calibration and programming, on-site technical setup, and light/loop playback management

caseStudy.brief: Forget-me-not is Victoria's first solo exhibition. It puts video on household objects instead of screens, and the set covers identity, archive, memory, aging, and home. It opened at St. Edward's University in February 2025 with five works listed by the artist: Forget-me-not, Entre Mundos, Sueños Rosas, 'Til Death Do Us Part, and Tender Cuts. It then moved to Ponte Creative Studio & Gallery, the Trucha RGV space at 1305 N Main St in McAllen, where it ran from 15 August to 16 October 2025. My part was the technical setup for the McAllen staging: fit Victoria's video onto the bed, the wall, the sink, and the window blind, and hold each object's image in place through the opening.
process: Victoria's video is the content. Each loop was matched to one surface before anything was mapped.
Surfaces were mapped in MadMapper. The bed, the sink, and the basin are not flat, so each mask was drawn on site against the real object rather than from a plan.
Resolume held the layers and the playback order. Each surface ran as its own clip, so one loop could restart without touching the rest of the room.
The sink scene also lights the floor in front of it. The spill reads as water under the basin and ties the object to the room.
The blind carries an orange figure at full height. The vertical strips in that image come from the blind, not from the video, which sets the scale.
Each work is its own clip on its own surface, so the room reads as a set of objects rather than as one image across the space.
House lights stayed low and the track heads were dimmed during playback, so the projected colour held its own value.
A playback check ran before opening: every clip, its in point, and its surface.
result: Two runs: St. Edward's University in February 2025, then Ponte Creative Studio & Gallery in McAllen, 15 August to 16 October 2025.
Six works in the McAllen show, one more than the first run. The room maps a bed, a wall, a sink, a basin, and a window blind.

projects.title: Meristem
projects.summary: A browser tool that grows an organic form from a typed seed, then exports it as a still, a vector, a solid mesh or a particle cloud.
projects.description: Five growth systems share one canvas: diffusion-limited aggregation, physarum, Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion, differential growth and space colonisation. Each grows from an integer seed, so any form is addressable by URL. Ink coverage picks a position on one of eight colour ramps, four stops each, and a band setting dithers between the tones, which turns a natural process into a printed gradient. Pause or finish the form and the volume exports unlock: a voxel mesh as GLB with vertex colours, a 25,000 to 400,000 particle cloud as PLY with per-particle colour, size and contour band, and a Bayer-dithered ASCII volume. One HTML file, no build step, no network after load.
projects.tools: Vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D, custom GLB and PLY writers

caseStudy.brief: Five natural growth processes had to share one canvas, so a form could be read as a still, a vector, a solid and a colour field without four separate tools. Each form had to come back from a number, and the printed output had to hold a real colour ramp rather than a single ink.
process: One canvas holds five systems: diffusion-limited aggregation, physarum, Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion, differential growth and space colonisation. Each writes into the same density grid, so the shared renderer, ramp and export read one field.
An integer seed drives mulberry32, and the same seed rebuilds the same form. The permalink carries the system, the seed and every shape parameter, so any form is addressable by URL.

Ink coverage picks a position on one of eight ramps, four stops each. The band setting dithers the ramp position between tones, not the colour, so a natural process prints as a gradient and not as one flat ink.

Pause or finish the growth and the volume exports unlock: a voxel mesh as GLB with vertex colours, a 25,000 to 400,000 particle cloud as PLY with per-particle colour, size and contour band, and a Bayer-dithered ASCII volume with one glyph per voxel.
The tool is one HTML file of 54,427 bytes. There is no build step and no network request after load, so it runs from a static host or a local folder.
Each system keeps its own parameter set, and the parameter list redraws when the system changes. Live parameter changes grow the form from the current step, and a restart replays it from the seed.
result: Five systems, eight colour ramps of four stops, and five exports: PNG at 2x, SVG, GLB, PLY and ASCII.
The whole tool is one 54,427-byte HTML file with no dependency and no build step.
At 1440 x 900 the form sits beside the control panel, and the panel scrolls. At 390 x 844 the form sits above the controls. Neither width scrolls sideways.

projects.title: Form Space
projects.summary: One valve rule carried into a whole space: 72 dithered forms, one centre and five rings of rising complexity, with any form opening as a volume of its own.
projects.description: Seventy-two forms share one rule set and one space. Each form is a valve: folds from 6 to 48, one to six rings, depth, edge sharpness, warp, quarter turns and a mirror. Complexity is computed from those values, so the field sorts itself into one centre and five rings, and a line joins each form to the closest simpler one. The same geometry renders as dither, ASCII or edges, and a click opens a form alone with its particle count. The renderer is three.js WebGPURenderer with TSL, and the page loads no image assets.
projects.tools: WebGPU, Three.js, TSL, Canvas 2D, Web Audio

caseStudy.brief: One valve rule had to carry a whole space: 72 forms that read as one family and still differ, arranged so a viewer can see the form change as the parameters rise. The space had to run full screen in a browser with no image assets, and any single form had to open as a volume of its own.
process: Every specimen comes from one valve rule: folds from 6 to 48, one to six rings, depth, edge sharpness, warp, a quarter turn and a mirror. The centre is the plain valve with no change.
Complexity is computed from the parameters, not assigned. Folds, ring count and warp give a value from 0 to 1, and the 72 specimens sort by that value, so the space reads as one ramp.

The layout puts one specimen at the centre and the rest on five rings of 7, 12, 16, 18 and 18. Each ring is one step of complexity. A line joins each specimen to the closest simpler one, which gives 71 links and a readable parent behind every form.
Each form is drawn as a dithered point cloud and as a valve outline from the same parametric surface. Nine palettes of three colours pass through one warm grey soften, so no form shouts.

Three render modes read the same geometry: dither, ASCII with a 10-glyph ramp, and edges. A sound toggle turns the five rings into five detuned drones with their own pan, and an opened form plays an arpeggio.

A click opens the form alone, fits the camera to the screen aspect, and prints its configuration name, fold count, ring count, warp and particle count. The name is read from the parameters, so the label follows the form and no list is stored.
result: 72 specimens, one centre, rings of 7, 12, 16, 18 and 18, and 71 links.
Nine palettes, three render modes and a five-ring sound bed.
The live lab runs at 60.6 fps at 1440 x 900 and 60.5 fps at 390 x 844. The case page recorded 60.0 fps at 1440 x 900 and 59.5 fps at 390 x 844.
On a portrait screen the camera fits to the aspect, so the outer ring runs past the frame and the field is read by orbit.

projects.title: Surveillance Status
projects.summary: Two public live cameras read by a browser vision model, with a language model writing a line for each tracked object.
projects.description: Two public camera feeds, one at the Zócalo in Mexico City and one at Times Square in New York. A browser vision model tracks each person and object, and a small language model writes one line for each. The overlay logs object IDs, position, velocity, and a status panel. The Mexico City cut writes in Spanish; the New York cut writes in English. The overlay is the work: boxes, IDs, velocities, and a line of prose over a live street.
projects.tools: MediaPipe, YOLOv8n, Web LLM, live camera

caseStudy.brief: Two public squares run through one browser pipeline. The Zócalo in Mexico City and Times Square in New York are already watched by cameras, phones, and algorithms. The piece adds a narrator. A vision model tracks each person and object, and a small language model writes one line for each. The line appears beside the box, in the language of the place. The feed is live, so each pass is a new cut. The overlay is the work: boxes, IDs, velocities, and a line of prose over a live street.
process: A public camera feed runs in the browser. The overlay prints its own log: objects tracked, motion level, and a velocity vector per object.
The vision pass assigns an ID to each person and object. Boxes and labels sit over the feed. The tracker keeps position and velocity for each ID.
Each label reports class, speed, and distance. The status panel prints the model, frame rate, object count, and a live list of IDs. The panel is part of the image, not a debug view.
A small language model writes one line for each tracked object. The prompt asks for one sentence in the language of the place. Mexico City writes in Spanish; New York writes in English.
The line sits beside the box. Long lines wrap; short lines leave space. The overlay stays legible at phone width.
The piece runs as one take. There is no narration, no cutaway, and no post-production overlay. The text arrives while the crowd moves.
The web cut is silent. The original post carries a soundtrack.
result: Two cities, two languages, one pipeline.
One logged frame reports 24 tracked objects, with a motion level and a velocity vector per object.
33.2 s Mexico City; 64.7 s New York.
The text is generated per object, not scripted per scene.
Each pass produces a different set of lines.

projects.title: River Pierce Foundation AR Showcase
projects.summary: A commissioned AR project for the River Pierce Foundation: a library of Carrizo Comecrudo objects and an 1871 San Ygnacio inscription.
projects.description: A commissioned augmented reality project debuted alongside The Teaching of the Hands experimental documentary screening and panel discussion at Treviño–Uribe Rancho in San Ygnacio, Texas.

links.label: The Teaching of the Hands event page

caseStudy.brief: The River Pierce Foundation commissioned an augmented reality project for its 2025 program at the Treviño–Uribe Rancho. The piece debuted on 10 May 2025 as the closing item of The Teaching of the Hands: a free screening of Carolina Caycedo and David de Rozas' documentary, then a panel with Carrizo Comecrudo representatives, then the AR at 3 pm. The content is specific to the place. Each object in the piece carries a panel that names its role in Carrizo Comecrudo practice, and a second reel sets the piece in San Ygnacio with a stone inscription dated 3 December 1871.
process: The brief was the place. San Ygnacio sits on the Rio Grande, and the rancho is a historic building held by the foundation under a Mellon Foundation Humanities in Place grant.

The content is interpretive rather than decorative. The bison skull is described as a symbol of life, sustenance, and respect, and the panel says the animal was not as central to Carrizo daily survival as it was for Plains cultures.
The bear carries its own panel: animals are treated as relatives and sources of strength, and bear skins are worn in a Carrizo Comecrudo ceremony called the Bear Dance.
The poles are named Xie Kua'k Kua̲m. The panel ties them to the four directions and to ceremonial use by the Carrizo.
A peyote cactus sits with a panel that quotes a peyote ceremony account and names Esto'k Gna culture.
The second reel sets five purple glyph discs above a bilingual inscription: La paz de Cristo sea con nosotros, 3 December 1871, S. Ygnacio ruega por nosotros.
The program fixed the schedule: screening at 1 pm, panel at 2 pm, AR debut at 3 pm, food by Malaquite at 3 pm.
The event was free and open to the public, so a visitor with no appointment had to be able to take part.
result: Two AR asset reels: 15.0 seconds at 1208 x 720, and 67.7 seconds at 1280 x 662.
Four objects and one inscription in the reels: bison skull, bear, prayer poles, peyote cactus, and the 1871 San Ygnacio text.
One commissioned AR piece, debuted 10 May 2025 in the 3 to 4 pm slot.
Venue: Treviño–Uribe Rancho, 604 Trevino St, San Ygnacio, TX 78067.

projects.title: 9ine5ive6eis
projects.summary: Visual identity for a limited apparel release: one cloud plate, a three-line lockup, a tee and a tote layout, and a brand motion loop.
projects.description: This project was an assignment to create the visual identity for a specific release within an ongoing apparel series. My contribution centered on the creation of the cloud graphic and custom typography, which was produced for a limited run on t-shirts and tote bags. I also created the accompanying brand motion graphic loop. This was a collaborative effort, with my work integrating into the final product photography provided by other artists.

caseStudy.brief: 9ine5ive6eis releases apparel in series, and each drop takes its own identity. This assignment covered one release: a cloud graphic, custom typography, a layout for a tee and a tote, and a motion loop for the brand. The run was limited. Other artists shot the product photography, so the identity had to survive their framing rather than a studio setup of our own.
process: The image is one sky photograph, cropped as a square plate. The plate is the whole graphic, with no second element and no frame.
The type is a three-line stack: 9INE, 5IVE, 6EIS, set wide and set small so it reads as a caption rather than a headline.
On the tee the plate sits at chest height and the type stays out. On the tote the plate runs the full width and the type sits inside the cloud at the lower right.
Both products are white, so the plate had to hold without a border to separate it from the garment.
A motion loop carried the same mark for the brand and ran beside the drop.
Product photography by other artists placed the pieces in daylight, on a skateboard and on a rooftop, which tested the plate against direct sun and moving cloth.
result: Two products in the run: a white tee and a white tote.
One three-line lockup, used at two scales.
One motion loop and one Instagram reel for the release.
Six product stills survive in the project file, from 130 KB to 660 KB each.

projects.title: Triqueta AR/VR Exhibition
projects.summary: AR poster designs, a VR scene built from Michael Flanagan's video works, and an immersive installation at the McAllen Creative Incubator.
projects.description: Triqueta was a collaborative exhibition project developed for the McAllen Creative Incubator. The project allowed me to develop and experiment with Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality, integrating them with the established artistic practice of filmmaker and artist Michael Flanagan. I focused on the technical development, creating a unique VR experience that incorporated Flanagan's video works, and building AR overlays for his original paintings, which also featured AI-generated elements. This installation explored the intersection of traditional painting, AI, and new media.
projects.tools: VR (Unreal), AR, and AI-assisted art. Collaborator: Michael Flanagan.

caseStudy.brief: Triqueta ran at the McAllen Creative Incubator in McAllen, Texas. The showcase carried AR poster designs, a VR experience, audio-visual installation, and generative digital art by regional artist and designer _selfsimilar_. Michael Flanagan's paintings and films were the collaborating body of work: his paintings took the AR overlays and his video became the VR scene. My part was development rather than authorship: build the technical layer that lets painted work be entered by a headset and by a phone, without the two reading as separate shows.
process: The work started from Flanagan's existing paintings and video, not from a new image.
Each painting carried an AR overlay. The overlays include AI-generated elements, which sit over the painted surface rather than replacing it.
The VR scene was built in Unreal and holds Flanagan's video works. A visitor in the headset sees the footage as the room, not as a screen on a wall.
Tracking used printed markers fixed to the wall beside each work. The reel shows a marker next to the poster it registers.
The overlays read as objects in the room, not as flat images. A dome sits in front of its poster and casts a shadow; slabs float off a wall.
The phone build and the headset build share one visual vocabulary, so a visitor who only uses the phone still reads the same project.
The room held three kinds of work at once: the AR posters, the headset station, and the generative and audio-visual installation.
result: Two modes in one room: AR on posters in a phone view, and a VR scene on a headset.
Venue: McAllen Creative Incubator, 601 N Main St, McAllen, Texas.

projects.title: Tigers Blood
projects.summary: A commissioned 3D animation of a static 2D logo, finished with a frosted metal material, analog video artefacts, and a print still for the 2023 show syllabus.
projects.description: Commissioned to create a dynamic digital asset from the client's static 2D logo. The process involved converting the original artwork into a 3D model, then applying a distinct lo-fi chromotype aesthetic with metallic textures and analog video effects. The final animation uses keyframed movement and a subtle glitch/vibration to transform the identity into a bold promotional graphic.
projects.tools: 3D modeling, texturing, lighting, animation, and compositing

caseStudy.brief: Tigers Blood had a flat 2D logo and a 2023 season to promote. The commission was a moving version of that mark: convert the artwork to 3D, give it a material that reads as metal under a bad signal, and keyframe a move that holds attention in a feed and on a poster. The finished animation ran with the show syllabus for the Rio Grande Valley dates, and the same geometry was shot as a print.
process: The 2D lettering was rebuilt as 3D geometry, keeping the hand-drawn spacing of the original rather than setting it in a typeface.
The glyphs sit on a ring instead of a baseline, so the mark can rotate without losing the word.
The material is a frosted metal with heavy grain. Highlights break up at the edges, which gives the lo-fi chromotype look.
The move is keyframed: a slow orbit that settles, with a small vibration on the settle so the mark never looks still.
A video pass adds analog artefacts: scan lines, chroma offset, and a soft edge.
The same geometry appears on burnt paper in the photograph of the printed sheet, so the animated and printed marks share one shape.
The clip and the printed sheet were produced separately.
result: One animated mark, one digital syllabus still, and one burnt-paper print, all carrying the same mark.
The 2023 syllabus still, 01.jpg at 720 x 1280, lists six dated entries across four venues: McAllen Convention Center, McAllen PAC, The Gremlin, and Cine El Rey.
02.jpg is a burnt-paper print at 1080 x 1350, listing seven dated entries: six at The Gremlin and one at Cine El Rey.
The animated mark is a hosted player clip at 1080 x 1080; its poster frame is assets/images/clips/IdbY_pPbY9G.jpg. No video file is stored in the repo.

projects.title: Motion
projects.summary: Self-set motion graphics studies in After Effects, Photoshop, and Blender: abstract form, procedural animation, and type built from repeating marks.
projects.description: A collection of personal experiments and studies in motion graphics, focused on exploring visual dynamics, abstract forms, and procedural animation techniques. These pieces were created as personal challenges to push the boundaries of my skills and test new concepts.
projects.tools: Adobe After Effects, Adobe Photoshop, and Blender

caseStudy.brief: Motion is a file of self-set studies, not a commission. Each study takes one visual idea and pushes it until the motion breaks: abstract form, procedural movement, and type drawn from repeating marks. The tools were After Effects, Photoshop, and Blender. There was no client brief and no delivery date. The point was to test a technique at speed and keep the result, so the file grew as a set of experiments rather than a body of finished work.
process: Each study opens with one form or one rule, not with a finished frame.
Type and shape were built in After Effects or Blender, then finished in Photoshop for grain and print texture.
The surviving still shows the method: a thin wave line sits above a letterform that fills from the top with a striped field, then turns into a dot grid at the base.
The work is designed as a loop, so the first and last frame have to match before the study counts as done.
The same form was reused at different densities, which is how one idea produced a short series rather than a single frame.
The export is a still. No loop survives in the project file today, so the case shows the still only.
result: One exported still survives in the project file. The number of studies in the set is unconfirmed.
The source still is 720 x 540 pixels and 209 KB on disk, at assets/images/motion.png.
The three case images, the still and two detail crops, total 430 KB.

projects.title: Collapsed Timelines In Felicitous Space
projects.summary: Technical setup for C. Díaz's 2022 exhibition at the McAllen Creative Incubator: four-channel video, a projected film, and a bilingual wall text.
projects.description: Technical setup for the exhibition at the McAllen Creative Incubator. The show paired a projected film with a four-channel video installation on monitors and a bilingual wall text, all inside a brick gallery with a low ceiling.
projects.tools: Four-channel video playback, monitors on plinths, projection alignment

caseStudy.brief: Collapsed Timelines In Felicitous Space ran from 4 to 26 March 2022 at the McAllen Creative Incubator, 601 N Main St, McAllen. C. Díaz built the show around California landscapes and geographical memory: the film Sacred Landscapes: The Arroyo Seco, the four-channel video installation Compressed Time, and the painting Body Landscapes No. 1. My part was the technical setup: four channels of playback on monitors, the projection, and the wall text that frames the room.
process: The show carried two video paths at once. One film played on the hanging screen, and Compressed Time ran across four monitors as a set rather than a mirror of one source.
Four channels need four sources and four start points, so the monitors were set up as separate players with a sync check before opening.
The monitors sit on white cylindrical plinths along the brick wall, with the cable runs on the floor behind them. That keeps the screens at seated eye height and leaves the floor clear.
The wall carries a bilingual projection of the film notes in Spanish and English. It is the first text a visitor reads on entering.
The projection was aligned to the screen and to the wall, then checked again with the house lights at event level.
The show closed on 26 March with a dialogue with sound artist Jon Almaraz and a deep listening session in the same room, so the space had to work as a screening room and as a listening room.
result: Four channels of Compressed Time on four monitors, one projected film, and one bilingual wall text in a single room.
Run: 4 to 26 March 2022 at the McAllen Creative Incubator, 601 N Main St, McAllen, TX 78501.
Three works in the show: Sacred Landscapes: The Arroyo Seco, Compressed Time, and Body Landscapes No. 1.

projects.title: Archived Works
projects.summary: One index for every study on the site, 2022 to 2026, with a link to each live page.
projects.description: Older studies and experiments, kept as a record. This page indexes every study on the site by year and links each one to its live page and case study.

caseStudy.brief: This page indexes the studies on the site in one place. It covers 2022 to 2026 and links each entry to its page. The hub groups the same thirteen studies by year, so the same set can be read two ways: by kind of project, and by date. Nothing here is a new piece. The value is the map: thirteen studies, four years, one link per study, and no dead ends.
process: Every entry is a project already on the site. No image on this page is new.
Rows are grouped by year, newest first: 2026, 2025, 2023, and 2022.
Each row carries a number, a title, a one-line summary, the discipline, the year, and a thumbnail.
The list is built from the site data file when the page loads, so one record feeds the work index, this index, and the study page.
Rows reuse the work-index component from the Work page, so the type scale, the hover state, and the thumbnail crop match the rest of the site.

A study is added with a record in the site data file and a page from the shared shell. Every list reads that one record, so the title, the discipline, and the year cannot drift. Each index numbers its own rows: Work counts down the sections, this index counts down the years.
The row preview is a gallery wall of framed works from the archive. The venue is unconfirmed.
Six clips from the archived pieces sit above the index, each with a poster frame. The player loads only when a clip is pressed.
The page opens on the work index row for this study, then numbered rows, the same layout as every other study page.
result: Thirteen studies indexed: four from 2026, four from 2025, three from 2023, and two from 2022.
Year range 2022 to 2026, read from the project records.
